scenes.narration: Cost-Optimized Architectures is worth twenty percent of the associate exam by itself, and it asks a different question than the other three domains. Instead of what makes this more resilient or more secure, it asks what's the smallest amount of money that still satisfies everything the scenario actually requires. Nearly every question in this domain tests one of exactly three ideas: is the resource sized correctly, does the workload's shape fit a given purchasing option, and which AWS tool actually answers a given cost question. This chapter builds all three, starting with the trap most candidates fall into first.

facts.label: Blueprint weight
facts.value: Design Cost-Optimized Architectures — 20% of the SAA-C03 Associate exam

facts.label: The rule underneath everything
facts.value: Right-size the resource first, then match a purchasing option to its shape

scenes.narration: Ask a room of candidates to optimize cost and the same reflexes show up constantly. Reach for a Reserved Instance or a Savings Plan first, because committing to spend feels like the obvious lever, without ever checking whether the instance underneath is even the right size. Treat Spot's steep discount as safe to use anywhere money is tight, without asking whether the workload can actually survive an instance disappearing on short notice. And apply one purchasing trick uniformly across an entire fleet, as if every workload inside it has the same shape. All three feel like diligence. All three skip the same step, and skipping it is exactly what makes them wrong.

props.heading: "Buy the discount first, worry about size later"
bullets: Commit to a Reserved Instance or Savings Plan before ever checking if the instance is the right size.
Treat Spot's deep discount as safe everywhere the budget is tight, regardless of interruption tolerance.
Apply one purchasing trick uniformly across a whole fleet instead of matching each workload's own shape.

scenes.narration: Here's the mechanism underneath both wrong reflexes. A purchasing option is a wrapper around a resource that already exists — it can't retroactively resize that resource, and it can't retroactively make an interruption-sensitive workload interruption-tolerant. So the check always runs in the same order. Gate one: is this resource actually sized for its real load, confirmed with real utilization data, not a guess. Only once that's settled does gate two apply: does the workload's duration and interruption tolerance actually match the purchasing option on the table. Committing to a multi-year Reserved Instance on an oversized instance locks in the waste for the length of the term. And treating Spot as free money without checking interruption tolerance ignores a real, fixed fact about the product — AWS can reclaim that capacity with two minutes' notice, whenever it needs it back.

props.heading: Two gates, always in this order
steps: Gate one: is the resource actually sized for its real utilization, backed by real data?
A purchasing discount multiplies whatever you're already paying — it never fixes an oversized instance
Gate two: does the workload's duration and interruption tolerance match the option on the table?
Spot's interruption notice is a fixed, real two minutes — a load-bearing fact, not an edge case
Jumping to gate two before clearing gate one is this domain's single most common wrong answer
Wire up governance tooling afterward, so a right answer today doesn't silently drift wrong next quarter

scenes.narration: Lay the four options side by side and one pattern explains all of them: each is trading certainty about your future usage for a discount. On-Demand gives AWS zero certainty and gets zero discount — and that's the correct, disciplined choice for anything genuinely new or unpredictable, not just the expensive option to avoid. Reserved Instances trade a one- or three-year commitment to a fairly specific configuration for a moderate discount, and optionally an actual capacity reservation. Savings Plans trade that same commitment length for a dollar-per-hour spend level instead, which keeps applying even as the instance family or size changes underneath it. And Spot trades away any guarantee at all, in exchange for the deepest discount of the four.

props.heading: Ranked by certainty traded for discount

rows.label: On-Demand
cells: None
Highest — stop or change anytime
Workload is new, short-lived, or not yet profiled

rows.label: Reserved Instances
cells: 1 or 3 years, fairly specific config

Steady usage you're confident about, especially if you need a zonal capacity reservation

rows.label: Savings Plans

scenes.narration: The exam never tests a specific discount percentage, because AWS adjusts them by instance family, region, and term length. What it does test, reliably, is the ordering, and the ordering never flips. Picture this as a relative index against On-Demand as the ceiling every other option discounts from: On-Demand sits at the top, Reserved Instances and Savings Plans sit in the middle within a broadly similar range of each other, and Spot sits at the bottom with the deepest discount of the four. No repricing event in AWS's history has ever made On-Demand cheaper than a matched commitment, or made a commitment cheaper than Spot for the same capacity. Memorize the shape of this chart, not a number sitting on it.

props.heading: Relative cost index — ordinal, not dollars

scenes.narration: Four real AWS tools, organized by the question each one actually answers. Cost Explorer's cost-and-usage call answers where has our money already gone, broken down by service or tag. Compute Optimizer's recommendation call answers gate one from a moment ago — is this specific resource the right size, based on real CloudWatch history behind it. Budgets' create-budget call is proactive alerting: tell me before spend crosses a threshold I've already defined. And checking Spot's price history before launch is the purchasing-side check for that fourth option. Confusing an analysis tool with an alerting tool is a common wrong-answer pattern on this exam.

props.heading: cost-governance/
lines: │   ├── get-cost-and-usage.sh       # Cost Explorer — where has the money gone
│   └── get-ec2-recommendations.sh  # Compute Optimizer — is this the right size
│   └── create-budget.json          # AWS Budgets — warn before overspend
└── describe-spot-price-history.sh  # real-time Spot signal before launch

scenes.narration: Three tools, three different questions, and the exam is really testing whether you can tell them apart from how a scenario is worded. Cost Explorer answers where has our money already gone — deep, account-specific, historical analysis. Budgets answers a narrower question: warn me before spend crosses a line I've already decided on. Trusted Advisor answers something broader and shallower — quick, rule-of-thumb recommendations available to every account with no custom analysis setup required. Free, generic advice is not the same as billing-specific analysis. A scenario asking for quick, broad recommendations wants Trusted Advisor; one asking for detailed analysis of your own specific spend wants Cost Explorer instead.

props.kicker: MATCH THE TOOL TO THE QUESTION

scenes.narration: Three commands map to the actual workflow a team runs after a cost signal fires. First, Cost Explorer's cost-and-usage call, grouped by service, to find out where the spend really went. Second, once a fleet is flagged, Compute Optimizer's recommendation call — the same gate-one right-sizing check from earlier, now as an actual API call, and it only works well once there's enough CloudWatch history behind the instance. Third, after right-sizing and picking a purchasing option, standing up a budget with an eighty-percent threshold closes the loop, so the same kind of drift gets caught automatically next time instead of showing up as a surprise on next month's invoice.

props.heading: From a spend signal to a fix

steps.cmd: aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-07-19,End=2026-08-18 --granularity DAILY --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE
output: Cost Explorer's underlying query, grouped by service
Turns "the bill went up" into "which service, which team"
Needs enough CloudWatch history behind it for a confident call
Threshold: 80% of the monthly EC2 budget
Notifies finops@example.com before the month closes out

scenes.narration: Take a concrete case. Ferro Analytics runs a large nightly batch job on a fleet of worker nodes that read from a queue, process a chunk of data, write results, and retry automatically if something fails. There's no fixed deadline within the night, and losing any one worker mid-task costs nothing but a retry. Run that through the two-gate check: interruption tolerance, not sizing, is the real open question here, and this workload clears it easily. So Spot Instances are the correct, cheapest answer, ideally spread across several instance types and Availability Zones so the whole fleet doesn't feel an interruption wave at once. Compare that to a fintech company running a single always-on transaction database with flat, predictable utilization for a year — same framework, completely different answer: a Reserved Instance or Savings Plan, because Spot is eliminated the moment a workload can't tolerate interruption.

props.heading: A nightly batch fleet that can lose any worker

profile.name: Ferro Analytics
profile.role: Nightly batch processing · horizontally-scaled queue workers · automatic retry on failure
profile.detail: Worker nodes read from a queue, process a chunk of data, and write results, retrying automatically on failure. There's no fixed deadline within the night, and losing a worker mid-task costs nothing but a retry.
profile.verdict: Spot Instances, spread across several instance types and Availability Zones. The workload is retryable, stateless, and interruption-tolerant — exactly Spot's target profile, and passing on its discount here would leave the cheapest correct answer on the table.

scenes.narration: Try these before we reveal the answers. First: a fleet has run at a steady twelve percent CPU utilization for six months, and a team wants to lock in a three-year Reserved Instance on the current instance size right now — what should actually happen first? Second, a step up in scope: an organization with dozens of linked accounts wants commitment discounts to apply everywhere, without every team buying and managing its own separate plan — what's the real mechanism that does that?

questions.prompt: An EC2 fleet has run at a steady twelve percent average CPU utilization for six months. A team proposes locking in a three-year Reserved Instance on the current instance size to save money right away. What should happen first?
options: Buy the Reserved Instance immediately — locking in a discount early is always the safer move.
Right-size the fleet using real utilization data before committing to any purchasing option.
Switch the fleet straight to Spot Instances instead of any commitment-based option.
Wait a full year for more billing data before doing anything at all.

questions.prompt: An organization has dozens of linked AWS accounts and wants commitment-based discounts to apply automatically across all of them, without every team buying and managing its own plan. What's the real mechanism?
options: Every linked account must purchase and manage its own separate Savings Plan.
A Savings Plan purchased at the management-account level can cover eligible usage across every linked account.
Reserved Instances are the only purchasing option that can apply across linked accounts.
Consolidated billing automatically converts On-Demand usage into a commitment once spend is high enough.

scenes.narration: Here's why. Twelve percent steady utilization is a loud signal the instance is oversized, and a three-year Reserved Instance made on top of that locks the waste in for the full term — right-sizing has to happen first, every time, before any purchasing decision gets made. And for the organization-wide question: a Savings Plan bought at the management-account level can cover eligible usage across every linked account at once, which is exactly how the discount applies everywhere without asking each team to buy and manage its own separate commitment.

answers.prompt: What should happen before locking in a three-year commitment on that steady twelve-percent fleet?
answers.correct: Right-size the fleet with real utilization data first, then choose a purchasing option.
answers.rationale: Twelve percent steady utilization is a strong signal the instance is oversized. A three-year commitment made before fixing that locks the waste in for the entire term — right-sizing always comes first, purchasing option second, never the reverse.

answers.prompt: How do commitment discounts apply across dozens of linked accounts without every team buying its own plan?
answers.correct: A Savings Plan purchased at the management-account level covers eligible usage across every linked account.
answers.rationale: Centralizing the commitment at the management-account level means no individual team has to purchase or manage its own Savings Plan — the discount applies automatically across the organization's combined eligible usage instead.

scenes.narration: Five things to carry forward. Right-size before changing a purchasing option, always in that order, never the reverse. Check interruption tolerance before reaching for Spot's discount, because a cheap answer that breaks the workload is still wrong. The relative ordering across the four options never flips even though the exact percentages do, so that ordering is what's actually worth memorizing. Match the governance tool to the specific question a scenario is asking, rather than reaching for whichever one sounds most sophisticated. And remember a fleet doesn't have to pick just one purchasing option — a steady baseline on a commitment with On-Demand or Spot layered on top for variable load is a legitimate, commonly correct pattern. props.heading: What to remember from this chapter
takeaways: Right-size before changing a purchasing option — always in that order, never the reverse.
Check interruption tolerance before reaching for Spot's discount; a cheap answer that breaks the workload is still wrong.
The ordering is stable even though the numbers aren't: On-Demand is the ceiling, Spot is the deepest discount, Reserved Instances and Savings Plans sit in between.
Match the tool to the question: Cost Explorer for where money went, Compute Optimizer for right-sizing, Budgets for proactive thresholds, Trusted Advisor for quick broad checks.
A fleet doesn't need one purchasing option — a steady baseline on a commitment plus On-Demand or Spot for variable load is a legitimate, common pattern.
